fixes.row: The wish of peace: “Grace and peace to you”, “Peace to you”, “All peace”
fixes.why: The label opens with the letters' formula 'Grace and peace' and the four examples are two Pauline openings, then Num 6:26 and Judg 19:20. The Hebrew blessing and greeting are the older speech and carry no 'grace' at all; they read as a footnote to an NT formula. Rule 5.
fixes.fix: Reorder the label to lead with the Hebrew speech: 'The wish of peace: “Peace to you”, “All peace”, “Grace and peace to you”'. Set eg to Num 6:26, Judg 19:20, Rom 1:7, 1 Cor 1:3 so the OT ones come first.

fixes.row: “Peace be with you”, “Peace I leave with you”, said by Jesus
fixes.why: The note says 'the verses do not name the speaker'. True of the verse alone, but the text supplies the speaker: both sit in the farewell speech of Jesus (John 13-17; 14:1 'believe in Me', 16:33 'in Me ... I have overcome the world'). The note manufactures doubt where the text has none, and it contradicts the row's own label ('said by Jesus'). Rule 1 (a note must not add or soften).
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: 'The first four name Jesus as the speaker. John 14:27 and 16:33 are in His farewell speech to the disciples (John 13-17).' Keep the door to Jesus.

fixes.row: “He”: our peace, who makes, proclaims or brings peace
fixes.why: Two different problems in one row. (a) Eph 2:14-15 follows Eph 2:13, which names Christ Jesus and the blood of Christ. Saying 'readers take it of the LORD, of the Messiah or of Christ' is false indeterminacy for an NT verse whose antecedent is in the text; every NT-reading seat would object. (b) Putting the Hebrew verses in the same row, under a note that closes on Christ and a door to Jesus, files Mic 5:5, Zech 9:10 and Isa 53:5 under an NT heading (rule 5). Each Hebrew verse has its own antecedent that the note hides: Mic 5:2,4 the ruler from Bethlehem who shepherds 'in the strength of the LORD' (distinct from the LORD); Zech 9:9 'your King comes'; Isa 53 the servant. Zech 9:10 and Mic 5:5 are read of the Messiah by Jewish readers as well, and 'of the LORD' is not a natural reading of either.
fixes.fix: Split in two. Row 1 (Hebrew first): '“He” in the prophets: the one who is our peace, who proclaims peace' with Mic 5:5, Zech 9:10, Isa 53:5; note: 'The text says “He”. In Micah he is the ruler from Bethlehem (5:2) who shepherds in the strength of the LORD (5:4); in Zechariah, the king who comes to Zion (9:9); in Isaiah, the servant. Readers take these of a king of David's line, of the Messiah, or of Jesus; of Israel, in Isaiah 53. The page does not choose.' Doors: Messiah only (no Jesus, no God). Row 2: 'He Himself is our peace' with Eph 2:14, Eph 2:15; note: 'Ephesians 2:13 names Christ Jesus; the verses speak of Him making the two one.' Door: Jesus.

fixes.row: “He”: our peace, who makes, proclaims or brings peace
fixes.why: Ps 147:14 is not an ambiguous 'He': the Psalm opens 'Exalt the LORD, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion' (147:12) and He strengthens the gates and blesses the children in the next verse. Listing it under a note that says readers take it of 'the Messiah or of Christ' misleads, and it is the same kind of verse as Num 6:26 or Ps 29:11, which are filed with the LORD.
fixes.fix: Move Ps.147.14 to 'From the LORD, from God' (by hand, as the divine persons are) and remove it from the He row. Add 'Ps 147:14 “He makes peace at your borders”, after 'Exalt the LORD' in 147:12' to that row's note if the verse is wanted visible.

fixes.row: “He”: our peace, who makes, proclaims or brings peace; Prince of Peace
fixes.why: The doors on these Hebrew verses are labelled 'Messiah / Christology (major theme)'. A reader of the Hebrew Scriptures meets 'Christology' as the frame for Isaiah 9 and Micah 5 before reading a word. The project's shown name for this theme is 'Messiah'. Rule 5.
fixes.fix: Show the door as 'Messiah' on every hub row; leave the id theme_messiah unchanged.

fixes.row: What peace stands beside: righteousness, justice, truth, love, joy, the law, life and blessing
fixes.why: 'Stands beside ... the law' reads as peace and the law as friendly companions (Ps 119:165 'peace belongs to those who love Your law'). Eph 2:15 says peace follows 'abolishing ... the law of commandments and decrees'. Listing it as a companion of the law is the opposite of what the verse says, and the note, 'where readers part on what is abolished', is the only thing keeping it from being a verdict. It is also the only verse that is there for 'the law' as an NT counterweight, which looks chosen. Rule 1 and rule 2.
fixes.fix: Take Eph.2.15 out of this row; it stands in the new Eph 2:14-15 row (see the He split) with its own note: 'Ephesians 2:15 says “abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees”; readers part on what is abolished, and the page takes no side.' Delete the Eph 2:15 sentence from this row's note. Keep Ps 119:165 and Mal 2:6 as the law's companions.

fixes.why: Two things the text supplies are missing. (a) The Greek the site reads has ἔχωμεν 'let us have peace' (subjunctive); the Berean prints 'we have peace' (ἔχομεν). The note is built on the indicative ('a verdict or a relationship') and the page shows the Berean's reading without the asterisk it uses elsewhere (the original arbitrates). (b) Job 22:21 is Eliphaz speaking; God says Eliphaz and his friends 'have not spoken rightly' (Job 42:7). Set beside Rom 5:1 and Isa 27:5 with no speaker named, it reads as the text's own teaching.
fixes.fix: Add to the note: 'In Romans 5:1 the Greek reads “let us have peace” and the Berean prints “we have peace”. Job 22:21 is Eliphaz speaking to Job.' Mark Rom 5:1 with an asterisk at the word and the finding beside it, as the site does for Mark 16 and John 7:53.

fixes.row: Seek it, pursue it, live in it: the way of peace, among the brothers, those who do good, being made holy
fixes.why: A reader under 'Seek it, pursue it, live in it' finds Rev 1:4, Col 1:2, 1 Thess 1:1, 1 Pet 1:2, Eph 6:23 and 1 Pet 5:14 (letter openings and closings, 'Grace and peace to you') and Acts 15:33 and 1 Cor 16:11 ('sent off in peace'). None of them says seek, pursue or live in peace. They are already in 'The wish of peace' and 'In peace' where they belong; they were swept in by the church rule. Rule 1 (label says only what its verses say).
fixes.fix: Remove these eight from the row (each is already in the wish row or the 'In peace' row). The row is then about 25 verses and its label is true of all of them.

fixes.row: Seek it, pursue it, live in it: ...; Safe, secure; welfare, well-being, prosperity
fixes.why: Deut 23:6 and Ezra 9:12 say 'You are not to seek peace or prosperity from them' (the Ammonites and Moabites) and 'Never seek their peace or prosperity'. Under a row labelled 'Seek it, pursue it' they read as the opposite of the label, and Deut 23:6 is the second lead example in 'Safe, secure; welfare' with no context. A reader sees an exclusion command offered as the first illustration of well-being, and a justice-attentive reader sees it with no note. Rule 1.
fixes.fix: Take both verses out of the 'Seek it' row; keep them in 'Safe, secure; welfare' but replace Deut 23:6 in eg with Ps 37:11 / Isa 54:13 / Job 5:24 (set eg to Gen 28:21, Jer 29:11, Ps 37:11, Josh 10:21) and add to that row's note: 'Deut 23:6 and Ezra 9:12 are commands not to seek the peace or prosperity of Ammon, Moab and the peoples of the land.'

fixes.why: Rule 6: three of the four lead examples (1 Chr 12:19, Gen 37:4, Gen 41:16) do not show the word 'peace' in English; the first example prints no word for the Hebrew at all, so the row opens on a verse that has no visible link to the concept. The note explains it, but a reader sees the examples first. Several verses in the row do read 'peace' plainly (Isa 33:7 'envoys of peace', Ps 55:18, Zech 6:13 'peaceful counsel', Song 8:10).
fixes.fix: Set eg to 2 Sam 17:3, Isa 33:7, Ps 55:18, Zech 6:13 (they show 'peace'); the verses with another Berean word stay in the list under the existing note.

fixes.why: The block's title says the words are 'translated “peace”', but for גְּמַר (h1585) the only verse is Ezra 7:12 and the Berean prints 'Greetings'; the example shows no peace. The report concedes this (MACULA's gloss only). The title is false for this entry.
fixes.fix: Drop h1585 from others (add to the spec's exclude list) or print it with a line 'the Berean prints “Greetings”'. Prefer dropping: it is one verse already covered by the wish row note.

fixes.why: Heb 12:11 is εἰρηνικός but the Berean prints 'a harvest of righteousness and peace' (the fruit of discipline). It is not peacemakers or people who are peaceable, so the example does not show its label. Also two different words (εἰρηνοποιός, εἰρηνικός) share the row.
fixes.fix: Relabel: 'Peacemakers (εἰρηνοποιός); peace-loving; the peaceful fruit of discipline (εἰρηνικός)' or set eg to Matt 5:9, Jas 3:17, Heb 12:11 with a note naming the two words.

fixes.row: Live at peace with one another, with everyone; “making peace through the blood of His cross”
fixes.why: The label promises the cross verse but the four examples (Mark 9:50, Rom 12:18, 2 Cor 13:11, 1 Thess 5:13) are all 'live at peace'; the one verse that makes the label heavy is hidden behind 'all'. Two different words (εἰρηνεύω, εἰρηνοποιέω) share a row. Rule 4 and rule 6.
fixes.fix: Set eg to Mark 9:50, Rom 12:18, 2 Cor 13:11, Col 1:20 (drop 1 Thess 5:13), and make the note name the two words: 'Live at peace is εἰρηνεύω; “making peace” in Col 1:20 is εἰρηνοποιέω.'

worker_points.point: 1. Rom 5:1 peace with God, justified through faith (verdict vs relationship)
worker_points.why: The no-side note is right in intent, but 'verdict or relationship' is a Protestant-forensic frame for a Catholic/Orthodox reader, and the note omits the ἔχωμεν / 'let us have' reading in the original. Add the textual finding and the Job 22:21 speaker (see fixes).

worker_points.point: 2. Isa 9:6-7 Prince of Peace as its own row, no door to Jesus
worker_points.why: It is a two-verse row, the note puts Hezekiah first, the OT verses are heard as a king's birth before anything else, and there is no Jesus door. Only the door name 'Christology' needs fixing (see fixes). The sentence is acceptable to the rabbi: it names Hezekiah and the Messiah as Jewish readings.

worker_points.point: 3. 'He' row (Mic 5:5, Eph 2:14-15, Ps 147:14, Zech 9:10): doors alone do not choose
worker_points.why: Doors do list all three possibilities, but the row itself misleads: Ps 147:14 is plainly the LORD, Eph 2:14 follows a verse naming Christ, and Micah and Zechariah each have an antecedent in their own context that is not the LORD. Split as in the fixes. Rule 5 is not met while Hebrew verses are filed in the same row as Ephesians under a Christ-closing note.

worker_points.point: 4. Gal 6:16 'the Israel of God' under 'Peace upon Israel', supersessionist/dispensational/Jewish readings differ
worker_points.why: The note names that readers part and takes no side, the OT verses lead the examples (Ps 125:5, 128:6), and the label quotes the verse's own word 'Israel'. Gal 6:16 is also in the wish row, where it is a blessing of peace and mercy. Acceptable to all eleven seats as it stands; the note says only that readers part, which is true.

worker_points.point: 5. Eph 2:15 abolishing the law, in the law row and the He row
worker_points.why: The note is fair but the row is wrong: 'stands beside the law' reads as friendly companionship and the verse says the law is abolished. Move the verse and the sentence to the Eph 2:14-15 row.

worker_points.point: 6. Luke 2:14 vs Matt 10:34 / Luke 12:51 set side by side
worker_points.why: All five verses are shown as written with Rev 6:4 and Luke 19:38, the note says the page does not decide how they fit, and every example shows the 'peace on earth' label.

worker_points.point: 7. John 14:27 and 16:33, speaker not named, door to Jesus
worker_points.why: Keep the door; the speaker is Jesus by the Gospel's own context (John 13-17). The note's doubt is the problem, not the door.

worker_points.point: 8. Col 1:20 and Job 22:21 reconciliation, atonement theories
worker_points.why: The no-side note on Col 1:20 is fine. Job 22:21 needs the speaker named (Eliphaz, whom God rebukes in 42:7), and the Col 1:20 verse should show among the examples (see fixes).

worker_points.point: 9. Divine-person rows by hand; 'peace of God, God of peace' now in the From-the-LORD pick row
worker_points.why: All three rows (said by Jesus, from the LORD/God, in Christ) are picks and name the person in the verse. The merge turned the one rule row into a pick, which is the better state under the by-hand rule. Only Ps 147:14 needs to join the LORD row, which is by hand and in the text's own named context. Isa 45:7's 'calamity' note is true to the Hebrew and fair; Job 25:2 (Bildad) is acceptable with the speaker note recommended for Job 22:21.

worker_points.point: 10. No Holy Spirit row for peace
worker_points.why: Right call. Gal 5:22 and Rom 14:17/15:13 stand under their own words in the 'stands beside' and 'faith' rows; no tradition is asked to accept a rule on πνεῦμα.
The merge dissolved it into the big 'Seek it' row, where the label 'being made holy' names the words only. The row's problem is the eight greeting verses (see fixes), not the sanctification verses.

The note says verses are listed as written and the page takes no side on what faith does. One point for the reader: Gal 5:22 'faithfulness' is the same Greek word as 'faith', which the text itself shows by the single word; no fix needed.

worker_points.point: 13. Berean's rendering of ambiguous Hebrew ('in triumph', 'wholly', 'a sound answer') kept in 'Peace in other uses'
worker_points.why: This is exactly the rule 4 care the hub was asked for: a different English word for the same Hebrew word is shown apart, with a note saying so. Only the order of the lead examples needs to change (see fixes).
The label says 'the city' and the note says Jer 29:7 is the city of the exile. A reader is not misled.

missing.what: The swords-into-plowshares and wolf-and-lamb pictures of peace, which use no word for peace and so are not in the hub; the Hebrew prophets' most-read peace texts are absent from a concept page that has 'Peace and war'. Could be a door or a 'pictures of peace' gather, not a row.

Quiet, rest and security by other Hebrew words (בֶּטַח, שָׁקַט), which the report notes as real neighbours; the 'Other words' block shows only four words and none for 'quiet', so a reader may think shalom is the whole of the Hebrew idea of peace as rest.
Shalem (שָׁלֵם), whole or complete, the cognate that makes 'wholehearted' (not 'peaceful'); not shown, so the reader does not see that shalom is a word of wholeness.

summary: The hub keeps the senses of שָׁלוֹם apart well (greeting, welfare, peace made between), puts the divine persons in by-hand rows, and keeps its notes neutral on Rom 5:1, Gal 6:16 and Luke 2:14 against Matt 10:34. It ships after thirteen fixes, chiefly splitting the 'He' row (Ps 147:14 is the LORD, Eph 2:14 follows Christ's name, Mic 5:5 and Zech 9:10 have antecedents of their own), naming the speaker in John 14:27 and Job 22:21, flagging the ἔχωμεν reading in Rom 5:1, and removing eight greeting verses from the 'Seek it' row.
